title: Glyoxylate and dicarboxylate metabolism
functional_summary: This module is anchored by several metabolites central to glyoxylate and dicarboxylate metabolism, including oxalic acid, oxalyl-CoA, and oxamate. Oxalic acid is a key end-product of glyoxylate metabolism, while oxalyl-CoA is an activated intermediate in the conversion of glyoxylate to oxalate. Oxamate is a structural analog of oxaloacetate and can act as an inhibitor of enzymes in this pathway, further supporting the module's focus on dicarboxylate transformations. The presence of malyl-CoA and related carboxylic acids suggests additional flux through TCA cycle intermediates and anaplerotic reactions. While glycocholate and aminopentol are present among the top metabolites, their roles are less directly connected to the core glyoxylate/dicarboxylate pathway and may reflect secondary or cross-pathway processes. Overall, the module is best explained by dysregulation of glyoxylate and dicarboxylate metabolism, with supporting evidence from both metabolite anchors and pathway coverage.

title: Glycerophospholipid and sphingolipid metabolism
functional_summary: This module is anchored by multiple early-ranked high-priority glycerophospholipids (e.g., 1-myristoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine, LysoPC(16:0/0:0), 1-dodecanoyl-glycero-3-phosphate, LysoPE(18:3(9Z,12Z,15Z)/0:0)) and sphingolipids (e.g., SM(d18:0/12:0), Cer(d18:0/18:0), Cer(d18:0/16:0), N-hexadecanoylsphinganine-1-phosphocholine). These metabolites are central intermediates in the remodeling, synthesis, and degradation of membrane phospholipids and sphingolipids, which are critical for membrane structure, signaling, and lipid transport. The presence of choline and related metabolites further supports active phosphatidylcholine turnover and choline-containing lipid metabolism. Pathway evidence from KEGG highlights strong coverage for choline metabolism and sphingolipid signaling, consistent with the observed metabolite classes. While some top metabolites (e.g., Borrelidin, Prostaglandin G2 2-glyceryl Ester, Tobramycin) are not directly related to these pathways and may reflect exogenous exposures or analytical noise, the dominant biochemical theme is clearly defined by the coordinated presence of glycerophospholipids and sphingolipids. Secondary signals from purine nucleotides and other minor classes are present but do not outweigh the lipid metabolism anchor.

title: Cysteine Catabolism and Sulfur Metabolism
functional_summary: This module is defined by the prominence of 3-sulfopyruvic acid and hydrogen sulfide, both central intermediates in the catabolism of cysteine and the broader sulfur metabolism network. The chemical class structure is dominated by carboxylic acids and derivatives, with pathway coverage strongly supporting cysteine and methionine metabolism, sulfur metabolism, and homocysteine degradation. The evidence points to active transsulfuration and sulfur amino acid turnover in cerebrospinal fluid. Several top-ranked metabolites (e.g., menatetrenone, 2,3-bis-O-(geranylgeranyl)glycerol 1-phosphate, deoxyhypusine) are not directly related to this pathway and likely represent peripheral, noise, or cross-pathway signals rather than core features of the module.

title: Thyroid hormone-related aromatic amino acid metabolism
functional_summary: The module is anchored by 3-(3,5-Diiodo-4-hydroxyphenyl)pyruvate and 3-(3,5-Diiodo-4-hydroxyphenyl)lactate, which are structurally related to iodinated derivatives of tyrosine and intermediates in thyroid hormone metabolism. These metabolites represent oxidative and reductive transformations of iodinated aromatic amino acids, reflecting steps in the peripheral metabolism of thyroid hormone precursors or degradation products. The presence of (4-bromophenylsulfanyl)pyruvate and other substituted aromatic acids further supports a theme of halogenated aromatic amino acid metabolism. While the module contains additional signals from plant-derived gibberellins and antibiotic-like compounds (epithienamycins), these are not central to the dominant biochemical process defined by the early-ranked, high-priority iodinated aromatic metabolites. The class-level structure and pathway evidence do not strongly support a canonical KEGG pathway, but the biochemical mechanism is consistent with host-mediated metabolism of iodinated aromatic amino acids and their derivatives.

title: Glucuronidation and conjugative metabolism
functional_summary: This module is anchored by several glucuronide and glucoside conjugates of diverse endogenous and exogenous compounds, including dihydrozeatin-O-glucoside, 3-methoxy-4-hydroxyphenylglycol glucuronide, 3',5'-diiodo-L-thyronine-beta-D-glucuronoside, and trichloroethanol glucuronide. These metabolites are products of phase II conjugative metabolism, primarily catalyzed by UDP-glucuronosyltransferases and UDP-glucosyltransferases, which attach glucuronic acid or glucose to a wide range of substrates to increase their solubility and facilitate excretion. The presence of steroidal (digoxin), flavonoid, isoflavonoid, and saccharolipid conjugates further supports a broad role for conjugation in the metabolism of both endogenous signaling molecules and xenobiotics. Pathway evidence from KEGG (pentose and glucuronate interconversions, amino sugar and nucleotide sugar metabolism) and HMDB (morphine and artemether metabolism) is consistent with this interpretation. While some top metabolites (e.g., Calenduloside E, Soyasapogenol A, Sativan) have limited pathway context, their occurrence as glycosides or glucuronides fits within the overall theme of conjugative metabolism.

title: Thiamine metabolism
functional_summary: This module is anchored by multiple early-ranked, high-priority metabolites directly involved in thiamine (vitamin B1) metabolism, including (7,8-dihydropterin-6-yl)methyl diphosphate(3-), (4-Amino-2-methylpyrimidin-5-YL)methyl dihydrogen phosphate, thiamine aldehyde, and several phosphorylated thiazole and pyrimidine intermediates. These compounds represent key biosynthetic and salvage pathway intermediates in the formation of thiamine and its active coenzyme forms, such as thiamine diphosphate. The presence of related azole and diazine derivatives, as well as thiazole and pyrimidine phosphate intermediates, further supports a focus on the enzymatic assembly and interconversion of thiamine precursors. The module also contains metabolites from the pteridine and pyridine classes, but these are consistent with the broader context of B-vitamin metabolism and do not outweigh the dominant thiamine pathway signal. KEGG and HMDB pathway evidence strongly support thiamine metabolism as the central biochemical process, with secondary overlap to vitamin B6 and riboflavin metabolism reflecting shared biosynthetic logic and cofactor interrelationships.

title: Pentose phosphate pathway
functional_summary: This module is anchored by a broad set of metabolites involved in the pentose phosphate pathway, as supported by high pathway coverage in both KEGG and HMDB. Early-ranked high-priority metabolites such as deoxyuridine (T6), guanosine (T8), inosine (T11), and cytosine (T14) are nucleoside and nucleotide derivatives that are products or intermediates of ribose metabolism and nucleotide biosynthesis, both of which are tightly linked to the pentose phosphate pathway. The class-level structure shows a high proportion of organooxygen compounds, including ribose and ribulose phosphates, sedoheptulose phosphates, and other sugar phosphates, which are canonical intermediates of this pathway. The pentose phosphate pathway provides ribose-5-phosphate for nucleotide synthesis and generates NADPH for reductive biosynthesis and antioxidant defense. While some top metabolites (e.g., N-Succinyl-L-citrulline, 5'-Dehydroadenosine, PQQH2) have limited direct annotation to this pathway, the dominant signal is defined by the nucleoside/nucleotide and sugar phosphate chemistry. Secondary signals from pyrimidine and purine metabolism are expected due to their biochemical integration with the pentose phosphate pathway.

title: Glycerolipid and glycerophospholipid metabolism
functional_summary: This module is anchored by high-priority glycerolipids (tripalmitin, diglyceride, DG(O-18:0/2:0/0:0), 1,2-dipalmitoyl-3-palmitoleoyl-sn-glycerol) and glycerophospholipids (PI(16:0/16:1(9Z)), PA(16:0/16:0), PE(P-16:0/16:0), PS(18:0/18:1(9Z)), PE(P-18:0/20:4(5Z,8Z,11Z,14Z)), LysoPC(24:0/0:0)), indicating a central role for the metabolism of complex lipids. title: Caffeine metabolism
functional_summary: This module is anchored by multiple purine nucleotides and imidazopyrimidine derivatives, with strong representation of caffeine and its related metabolites. Supporting metabolites such as hypoxanthine and inosine reflect downstream purine catabolism, which is biochemically linked to caffeine degradation. While ribose-1-arsenate and diethyl glutarate are present among the top metabolites, their limited pathway and class context suggest they are peripheral or reflect cross-pathway activity rather than central to the module's dominant biochemical process.

title: Glycerophospholipid metabolism

functional_summary: This module is anchored by multiple high-priority metabolites involved in galactose metabolism, including D-Galactono-1,5-lactone, UDP-N-acetylmuraminate, and several sphingolipids with galactosyl moieties. title: Pyrimidine metabolism
functional_summary: This module is anchored by high-priority pyrimidine nucleotides such as dTDP(3-) and UTP(4-), supported by additional pyrimidine nucleotides and nucleosides throughout the module. title: Arachidonic acid metabolism
functional_summary: This module is anchored by multiple early-ranked high-priority metabolites involved in arachidonic acid metabolism, including 15(R)-hydroperoxy-EPE, Thromboxane B2, 13,14-Dihydro-15-keto PGF2a, and 11-Dehydro-thromboxane B2. These metabolites represent key intermediates and products of the enzymatic oxidation of arachidonic acid and related polyunsaturated fatty acids, leading to the formation of prostaglandins, thromboxanes, and hydroperoxy derivatives. The pathway involves cyclooxygenase and lipoxygenase activities, generating bioactive lipid mediators that regulate inflammation, vascular tone, and platelet aggregation. The presence of glutathione disulfide(2-) and 3-disulfanyl-L-alanine zwitterion suggests active redox cycling and detoxification processes, which are integral to the metabolism and inactivation of reactive lipid peroxides. While some top metabolites such as copalyl diphosphate and ent-copalyl diphosphate are not directly related to this pathway, the overwhelming class-level structure and pathway coverage support arachidonic acid metabolism as the dominant biochemical process.
